frontHtml: Coagulase-negative staphylococcus, novobiocin resistant, causing cystitis in a young sexually active woman?
backHtml: Staphylococcus saprophyticus (nitrite test often negative).

frontHtml: Which E. coli adhesin is most linked to ascending pyelonephritis?
backHtml: P fimbriae (bind galactose-containing glycolipids on uroepithelium). Type 1 (mannose-binding) fimbriae favour bladder colonisation.

frontHtml: Alkaline urine (pH above 7.5) and a staghorn calculus suggest what kind of organism and stone?
backHtml: A urease producer (classically Proteus mirabilis) and struvite: magnesium ammonium phosphate.

frontHtml: Which urine microscopy finding places an infection in the kidney rather than the bladder?
backHtml: White blood cell casts: casts form only in renal tubules.

frontHtml: Sterile pyuria with hematuria and moth-eaten calyces: likely diagnosis and test?
backHtml: Genitourinary tuberculosis; acid-fast culture and nucleic acid testing of several first-morning urine samples.

frontHtml: Bladder cancer type after chronic Schistosoma haematobium infection?
backHtml: Squamous cell carcinoma (after squamous metaplasia). Treat the infection with praziquantel.

frontHtml: Staghorn stone, nonfunctioning kidney and foamy lipid-laden macrophages that mimic a tumour?
backHtml: Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (Proteus or E. coli); usually nephrectomy.

frontHtml: Kidney transplant recipient, rising creatinine, urine "decoy cells" with intranuclear inclusions: cause and first step?
backHtml: BK polyomavirus nephropathy; reduce immunosuppression.

frontHtml: First-line options for acute uncomplicated cystitis in a nonpregnant woman?
backHtml: Nitrofurantoin 5 days; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 3 days (if resistance below about 20%); single-dose fosfomycin; pivmecillinam. No culture needed for a first typical episode.

frontHtml: Why is nitrofurantoin wrong for pyelonephritis?
backHtml: It concentrates in urine but does not reach adequate kidney tissue or blood levels.

frontHtml: When is asymptomatic bacteriuria treated?
backHtml: Pregnancy (screen once early with culture) and before a urologic procedure that breaches the mucosa. Not in older adults, diabetes or catheters.

frontHtml: Septic patient with an obstructing ureteral stone and infected urine: next step after antibiotics?
backHtml: Urgent decompression (ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy); definitive stone treatment later.

frontHtml: Gas in the renal parenchyma of a patient with diabetes and pyelonephritis: management?
backHtml: Emphysematous pyelonephritis: IV antibiotics plus percutaneous drainage; nephrectomy if no improvement.

frontHtml: Pyelonephritis in pregnancy: setting and drug?
backHtml: Admit; IV beta-lactam such as ceftriaxone; then suppression or culture surveillance until delivery.

frontHtml: Catheter-associated UTI in a catheter in place for more than 2 weeks: what before antibiotics?
backHtml: Remove or replace the catheter and culture urine from the new catheter (never from the bag).

frontHtml: Gross hematuria 1–2 days after a sore throat, normal C3: diagnosis and deposit site?
backHtml: IgA nephropathy; mesangial IgA deposits.

frontHtml: Hematuria 1–3 weeks after pharyngitis or 3–6 weeks after impetigo, low C3: diagnosis and EM finding?
backHtml: Post-streptococcal GN; large subepithelial humps.

frontHtml: Target antigen in anti-GBM disease?
backHtml: Noncollagenous domain of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen (linear IgG on IF).

frontHtml: Which three groups does immunofluorescence sort crescentic GN into?
backHtml: Linear (anti-GBM), granular (immune complex: lupus, IgA, post-infectious), pauci-immune (ANCA).

frontHtml: Lupus nephritis class with subendothelial "wire-loop" deposits in half or more of glomeruli?
backHtml: Class IV (diffuse proliferative).

frontHtml: Low C3 with normal C4 and C3-dominant deposits without infection: diagnosis and mechanism?
backHtml: C3 glomerulopathy; e.g., C3 nephritic factor stabilising C3bBb (alternative pathway).

frontHtml: Hepatitis C, palpable purpura, positive rheumatoid factor and very low C4 with an MPGN pattern?
backHtml: Cryoglobulinemic glomerulonephritis.

frontHtml: Hematuria, sensorineural deafness, anterior lenticonus and a split GBM?
backHtml: Alport syndrome: type IV collagen defect, most often X-linked COL4A5.

frontHtml: Normal light microscopy, negative IF, effaced foot processes?
backHtml: Minimal change disease.

frontHtml: Antibody found in most primary membranous nephropathy?
backHtml: Anti-phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R).

frontHtml: HIV with nephrotic syndrome and large echogenic kidneys: lesion and genetic risk factor?
backHtml: Collapsing FSGS; two APOL1 risk variants.

frontHtml: Why are nephrotic patients hypercoagulable?
backHtml: Urinary loss of antithrombin (and proteins C and S) plus increased hepatic fibrinogen and factor synthesis.

frontHtml: Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesion?
backHtml: Nodular PAS-positive mesangial sclerosis of diabetic nephropathy.

frontHtml: Congo red with apple-green birefringence in a patient with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis: protein?
backHtml: AA amyloid (from serum amyloid A).

frontHtml: Drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis: hypersensitivity type and urine findings?
backHtml: Type IV (T cell); sterile pyuria, white cell casts, sometimes urine eosinophils.

frontHtml: ANCA-positive rapidly progressive GN: induction therapy?
backHtml: Glucocorticoids plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide, started without waiting for biopsy.

frontHtml: Anti-GBM disease: treatment?
backHtml: Urgent plasma exchange plus glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide.

frontHtml: First-line treatment of IgA nephropathy with proteinuria?
backHtml: Maximal tolerated ACE inhibitor or ARB, blood pressure control, SGLT2 inhibitor when eGFR allows.

frontHtml: Lupus patient: when to biopsy the kidney?
backHtml: Proteinuria about 0.5 g/day or more, an active sediment, or an unexplained rise in creatinine.

frontHtml: Class IV lupus nephritis induction, and the change before pregnancy?
backHtml: Glucocorticoids plus mycophenolate (or low-dose cyclophosphamide); switch mycophenolate to azathioprine and continue hydroxychloroquine.

frontHtml: Child aged 1–10 years with typical nephrotic syndrome: first step?
backHtml: Oral glucocorticoids without biopsy (presumed minimal change).

frontHtml: PLA2R-negative membranous nephropathy in an older smoker with weight loss: next step?
backHtml: Search for a secondary cause, especially cancer (chest CT, age-appropriate screening).

frontHtml: Nephrotic patient with sudden flank pain, hematuria and raised LDH: diagnosis and test?
backHtml: Renal vein thrombosis; CT or MR venography, then anticoagulation.

frontHtml: Suspected drug-induced AIN: first step?
backHtml: Stop the drug; glucocorticoids if no improvement within several days or severe injury.

frontHtml: ADPKD genes, chromosomes and which is more severe?
backHtml: PKD1 (chromosome 16, polycystin-1; about 80%, earlier kidney failure) and PKD2 (chromosome 4, polycystin-2; milder).

frontHtml: Where do polycystins act, and what second messenger drives ADPKD cyst growth?
backHtml: Primary cilium of tubular cells; low intracellular calcium raises cAMP, which drives proliferation and fluid secretion.

frontHtml: Most common extrarenal manifestation of ADPKD?
backHtml: Liver cysts. Others: berry aneurysms, mitral valve prolapse, colonic diverticula, hernias.

frontHtml: ARPKD: gene, renal pattern and obligatory liver lesion?
backHtml: PKHD1 (fibrocystin); radially dilated collecting ducts with large echogenic kidneys; congenital hepatic fibrosis.

frontHtml: Many cysts in small, scarred kidneys after years of dialysis: name and risk?
backHtml: Acquired cystic kidney disease; raised risk of renal cell carcinoma.

frontHtml: Normal-sized kidneys, recurrent calcium stones, brush-like contrast streaks in the papillae?
backHtml: Medullary sponge kidney (dilated medullary collecting ducts); function usually preserved.

frontHtml: Three tissues of an angiomyolipoma, and the syndrome when tumours are multiple and bilateral?
backHtml: Mature fat, smooth muscle, thick-walled vessels; tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC1/TSC2, mTORC1 overactivity).

frontHtml: Renal oncocytoma: cell of origin, gross look and ultrastructure?
backHtml: Collecting duct intercalated cells; mahogany brown with a central stellate scar; cells packed with mitochondria.

frontHtml: Why does early ADPKD cause hypertension before GFR falls?
backHtml: Cysts compress intrarenal vessels, causing ischemia and renin-angiotensin activation.

frontHtml: Bosniak I/II, IIF, III, IV: what to do?
backHtml: I/II: nothing. IIF: imaging surveillance. III/IV: surgical excision (often partial nephrectomy), or surveillance if a poor surgical candidate.

frontHtml: First-line antihypertensive in ADPKD?
backHtml: ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker (plus sodium restriction and good water intake).

frontHtml: Tolvaptan in ADPKD: who gets it and what must be monitored?
backHtml: Adults at risk of rapid progression (large kidney volume for age, fast eGFR fall); monitor liver tests (hepatotoxicity).

frontHtml: Antibiotic choice for an infected renal cyst in ADPKD?
backHtml: A lipid-soluble, cyst-penetrating agent: fluoroquinolone or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, for several weeks; drain if no response.

frontHtml: Which ADPKD patients get screening for intracranial aneurysm, and with what?
backHtml: Family history of aneurysm or SAH, prior rupture, high-risk job, major elective surgery; MR angiography.

frontHtml: Hemodynamically responsive patient with active bleeding from a renal angiomyolipoma: treatment?
backHtml: Selective arterial embolisation (kidney-sparing).

frontHtml: Most common renal cell carcinoma subtype, cell of origin and chromosome change?
backHtml: Clear cell (about 70–75%), proximal tubule, loss of 3p with VHL inactivation.

frontHtml: What does the VHL protein normally do?
backHtml: It is part of an E3 ubiquitin ligase that targets HIF for degradation when oxygen is present; loss lets HIF drive VEGF.

frontHtml: Which chromosomal and gene changes go with papillary renal cell carcinoma?
backHtml: Sporadic tumours often gain chromosomes 7 and 17; the hereditary papillary form carries activating MET variants.

frontHtml: Renal medullary carcinoma occurs in which population?
backHtml: Young people with sickle cell trait; highly aggressive.

frontHtml: Four paraneoplastic hormones of renal cell carcinoma?
backHtml: Erythropoietin (polycythemia), PTHrP (hypercalcemia), renin (hypertension), ACTH (Cushing syndrome).

frontHtml: Why can renal cell carcinoma cause a left varicocele that persists when lying down?
backHtml: The left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein, which the tumour can obstruct.

frontHtml: Adverse effects of VEGF receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors used for RCC?
backHtml: Hypertension, proteinuria, hand-foot skin reaction, diarrhea, hypothyroidism, poor wound healing.

frontHtml: Wilms tumour: histology pattern and cell of origin?
backHtml: Triphasic (blastema, epithelium, stroma); persistent metanephric blastema.

frontHtml: WAGR syndrome genetics?
backHtml: 11p13 deletion removing WT1 and PAX6 (Wilms, aniridia, GU anomalies, developmental delay).

frontHtml: Beckwith-Wiedemann: locus, mechanism and tumours?
backHtml: 11p15.5 imprinting defect (often IGF2 overexpression); Wilms tumour and hepatoblastoma.

frontHtml: Leading risk factor for urothelial carcinoma, and occupational carcinogens?
backHtml: Cigarette smoking; aromatic amines (benzidine, 2-naphthylamine) in dye, rubber and leather work.

frontHtml: Cyclophosphamide bladder toxin and its antidote?
backHtml: Acrolein (hemorrhagic cystitis, bladder cancer); mesna plus hydration.

frontHtml: Bladder adenocarcinoma at the dome suggests what origin?
backHtml: A urachal remnant.

frontHtml: Gross hematuria in a smoker on an anticoagulant: evaluation?
backHtml: CT urography plus cystoscopy; anticoagulation does not explain hematuria.

frontHtml: Small (up to 4 cm) localised renal mass in a fit patient: treatment?
backHtml: Partial (nephron-sparing) nephrectomy; ablation or surveillance if frail.

frontHtml: Bladder cancer: non-muscle-invasive high grade vs muscle-invasive treatment?
backHtml: NMIBC high grade or CIS: TURBT then intravesical BCG. MIBC: neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy then radical cystectomy.

frontHtml: First-line systemic therapy for metastatic clear cell RCC?
backHtml: Immune checkpoint inhibitor-based combination (PD-1 inhibitor plus VEGFR TKI, or nivolumab plus ipilimumab).

frontHtml: Which proteins does the dipstick protein pad detect best, and which does it miss?
backHtml: Albumin; it misses light chains and other low-molecular-weight proteins.

frontHtml: Dysmorphic red cells (acanthocytes) and red cell casts: source of hematuria?
backHtml: Glomerular.

frontHtml: Hematuria with clots: glomerular or nonglomerular?
backHtml: Nonglomerular (urinary tract below the glomerulus); clots argue against glomerular bleeding.

frontHtml: Heme-positive dipstick, no red cells, clear plasma, very high CK?
backHtml: Myoglobinuria from rhabdomyolysis.

frontHtml: Heme-positive dipstick, no red cells, pink plasma, low haptoglobin?
backHtml: Hemoglobinuria from intravascular hemolysis.

frontHtml: Beta-2 microglobulin in urine with little albumin: what kind of proteinuria and where is the lesion?
backHtml: Tubular proteinuria; proximal tubule.

frontHtml: Muddy brown granular casts?
backHtml: Acute tubular necrosis.

frontHtml: Waxy and broad casts?
backHtml: Advanced chronic kidney disease (stasis in dilated atrophic tubules).

frontHtml: Maltese-cross bodies under polarised light in urine?
backHtml: Oval fat bodies (lipiduria) of nephrotic syndrome.

frontHtml: Hexagonal urine crystals?
backHtml: Cystine (cystinuria).

frontHtml: Urine that turns black on standing, dark ear cartilage, early arthritis?
backHtml: Alkaptonuria: homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase deficiency.

frontHtml: Polyuria with urine osmolality at or above plasma osmolality?
backHtml: Solute (osmotic) diuresis: glucose, urea, mannitol, saline.

frontHtml: Painless hematuria and a urine concentrating defect in a young person with HbS 40%?
backHtml: Sickle cell trait (medullary sickling, papillary injury).

frontHtml: Definition of microscopic hematuria?
backHtml: 3 or more red cells per high-power field on microscopy of a properly collected specimen.

frontHtml: High-risk microscopic hematuria (age 60+, more than 30 pack-years, more than 25 RBC/hpf, or any gross hematuria): evaluation?
backHtml: Cystoscopy and CT urography.

frontHtml: Does anticoagulation explain hematuria?
backHtml: No; evaluate as for any patient.

frontHtml: Isolated low-grade proteinuria in a healthy adolescent: first test?
backHtml: First-morning urine (or split upright and recumbent collection) for orthostatic proteinuria.

frontHtml: Sudden oliguria in an older man on anticholinergics or opioids: first step?
backHtml: Bladder scan and catheterisation to relieve retention.

frontHtml: Efferent arteriolar constriction (angiotensin II): effect on RPF, GFR and filtration fraction?
backHtml: RPF down, GFR up (modestly), filtration fraction up.

frontHtml: NSAIDs affect glomerular hemodynamics how?
backHtml: Block prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilation: RPF and GFR fall, filtration fraction about unchanged.

frontHtml: Clearance formula?
backHtml: C = (U × V) / P. Inulin clearance = GFR; PAH clearance ≈ effective renal plasma flow.

frontHtml: Why does creatinine clearance slightly overestimate GFR?
backHtml: Creatinine is also secreted by the proximal tubule.

frontHtml: Which nephron segment and transporter do thiazides block, and what happens to urine calcium?
backHtml: Distal convoluted tubule NCC (Na⁺-Cl⁻ cotransporter); urine calcium falls.

frontHtml: Urine indices of prerenal AKI?
backHtml: FENa below 1%, urine Na below 20 mEq/L, urine osmolality above 500, BUN:Cr above 20, bland sediment.

frontHtml: Urine sediment of acute tubular necrosis?
backHtml: Muddy brown granular casts and renal tubular epithelial cells; FENa above 2%.

frontHtml: Which nephron segments are most vulnerable to ischemic ATN?
backHtml: Straight proximal tubule and medullary thick ascending limb.

frontHtml: Dipstick 3+ blood, almost no red cells on microscopy?
backHtml: Myoglobinuria (rhabdomyolysis) or hemoglobinuria.

frontHtml: Mineral pattern of CKD-mineral bone disorder?
backHtml: High phosphate and FGF23, low calcitriol, low calcium, high PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism).

frontHtml: Arteriolar lesion of malignant hypertension versus long-standing benign hypertension?
backHtml: Malignant: hyperplastic (onion-skin) arteriolosclerosis with fibrinoid necrosis. Benign: hyaline arteriolosclerosis.

frontHtml: Radiolucent kidney stone in acidic urine?
backHtml: Uric acid; prevent with potassium citrate (urine pH about 6–6.5).

frontHtml: Hexagonal crystals in urine?
backHtml: Cystine (cystinuria: defective proximal reabsorption of cystine, ornithine, lysine, arginine).

frontHtml: Why does ileal disease cause calcium oxalate stones?
backHtml: Fatty acids bind luminal calcium, leaving oxalate free to be absorbed in the colon (enteric hyperoxaluria).

frontHtml: Type 1 (distal) RTA: potassium, urine pH, stones?
backHtml: Hypokalemia; urine pH above 5.5; calcium phosphate stones and nephrocalcinosis.

frontHtml: Type 4 RTA: cause and potassium?
backHtml: Low aldosterone effect (often hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism in diabetes, or drugs); hyperkalemia; urine pH below 5.5.

frontHtml: Glycosuria with normal blood glucose, hypophosphatemia, hypouricemia and acidosis?
backHtml: Fanconi syndrome (proximal tubule); causes include tenofovir, ifosfamide, myeloma, Wilson disease, cystinosis.

frontHtml: Hypertension, hypokalemia, low renin and low aldosterone, responds to amiloride?
backHtml: Liddle syndrome (ENaC gain of function).

frontHtml: Bartter versus Gitelman: urine calcium and magnesium?
backHtml: Bartter (thick ascending limb): high urine calcium. Gitelman (DCT): low urine calcium and hypomagnesemia.

frontHtml: KDIGO definition of AKI?
backHtml: Creatinine up at least 0.3 mg/dL in 48 h, or at least 1.5 × baseline within 7 days, or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h.

frontHtml: Indications for urgent dialysis?
backHtml: Refractory acidosis, refractory hyperkalemia, dialysable poisons, refractory volume overload, uremic pericarditis, encephalopathy or bleeding.

frontHtml: Tumor lysis prevention in a high-risk patient?
backHtml: IV fluids plus rasburicase (check G6PD first); allopurinol for intermediate risk.

frontHtml: How does KDIGO grade albuminuria by urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio?
backHtml: A1: under 30 mg/g (normal to mildly raised). A2: 30 to 300 mg/g (moderately raised). A3: over 300 mg/g (severely raised).

frontHtml: Type 2 diabetes with CKD and persistent albuminuria on max ACE inhibitor/ARB plus SGLT2 inhibitor, normal potassium: next drug?
backHtml: Finerenone (if eGFR at least 25).

frontHtml: Anemia of CKD: what before an ESA, and what hemoglobin target to avoid?
backHtml: Replete iron first; avoid targeting 13 g/dL or more (stroke, thrombosis).

frontHtml: Uncomplicated distal ureteral stone 5–10 mm: treatment?
backHtml: Trial of passage with an NSAID and tamsulosin; strain urine; remove if not passed in about 4–6 weeks.

frontHtml: Recurrent calcium stones with hypercalciuria: prevention?
backHtml: Fluids (urine above 2.5 L/day), low sodium, normal calcium intake, thiazide.

frontHtml: Best imaging for suspected kidney stone, and the exception?
backHtml: Noncontrast low-dose CT; ultrasound first in pregnancy and children.

frontHtml: Three triggers of renin release from juxtaglomerular cells?
backHtml: Low afferent arteriolar pressure, low NaCl delivery to the macula densa, and sympathetic beta-1 stimulation.

frontHtml: Unilateral renal artery stenosis: renin, aldosterone and potassium?
backHtml: High renin, high aldosterone (secondary), low potassium; renin lateralises to the stenotic kidney.

frontHtml: Atherosclerotic vs fibromuscular renal artery stenosis: location?
backHtml: Atherosclerotic: ostium and proximal artery. Fibromuscular dysplasia: mid and distal artery.

frontHtml: "String of beads" renal artery in a young woman?
backHtml: Fibromuscular dysplasia (usually medial fibroplasia).

frontHtml: Why does GFR fall after an ACE inhibitor in renal artery stenosis?
backHtml: Loss of angiotensin II constriction of the efferent arteriole lowers glomerular capillary pressure.

frontHtml: Benign nephrosclerosis: vessel lesion and gross kidney?
backHtml: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis; small, symmetric, finely granular kidneys.

frontHtml: Malignant nephrosclerosis: vessel lesions and gross kidney?
backHtml: Hyperplastic (onion-skin) arteriolosclerosis and fibrinoid necrosis; flea-bitten petechial surface.

frontHtml: Gross and microscopic appearance of an embolic renal infarct?
backHtml: Pale, wedge-shaped, base on the capsule; coagulative necrosis.

frontHtml: Cholesterol emboli: biopsy finding and clinical clues?
backHtml: Biconvex needle-shaped clefts in small arteries; livedo, blue toes with pulses, eosinophilia, low complement, weeks after a procedure.

frontHtml: Nephrotic syndrome most linked to renal vein thrombosis, and one mechanism?
backHtml: Membranous nephropathy; urinary loss of antithrombin (plus more hepatic procoagulants).

frontHtml: New left varicocele with nephrotic syndrome?
backHtml: Left renal vein thrombosis (left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein).

frontHtml: Risk factors for scleroderma renal crisis?
backHtml: Early diffuse cutaneous disease, anti-RNA polymerase III, high-dose glucocorticoids.

frontHtml: Clues to renovascular hypertension?
backHtml: Onset before 30 or new severe hypertension after 55, creatinine rise above about 30% on ACE inhibitor/ARB, flash pulmonary edema, asymmetric kidneys, abdominal bruit.

frontHtml: Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis with controlled BP and stable creatinine: management?
backHtml: Optimal medical therapy (BP control including ACE inhibitor/ARB, statin, antiplatelet, smoking cessation); no routine stenting.

frontHtml: Revascularisation triggers in atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis?
backHtml: Recurrent flash pulmonary edema, rapidly falling kidney function from the stenosis, truly refractory hypertension.

frontHtml: Fibromuscular dysplasia with hypertension: treatment?
backHtml: Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty without stenting; image head-to-pelvis arteries once.

frontHtml: Scleroderma renal crisis: treatment?
backHtml: Captopril titrated rapidly; continue even with rising creatinine or dialysis.

frontHtml: Flank pain, hematuria, very high LDH, normal noncontrast CT in atrial fibrillation: next test and treatment?
backHtml: Contrast CT (CT angiography) for renal infarction; anticoagulation.

frontHtml: Which autonomic outflow contracts the detrusor, and through which receptor?
backHtml: Parasympathetic S2–S4 (pelvic splanchnic nerves) via muscarinic M3 receptors.

frontHtml: Sympathetic receptors that help the bladder store urine?
backHtml: Beta-3 relaxes the detrusor; alpha-1 closes the bladder neck and internal sphincter (T10–L2, hypogastric nerve).

frontHtml: Bladder pattern after spinal cord injury between the pons and the sacral cord?
backHtml: Detrusor overactivity with detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia: high pressures, reflux, hydronephrosis.

frontHtml: Bladder pattern with a lesion above the pons (stroke, dementia)?
backHtml: Detrusor overactivity (urge incontinence) with coordinated sphincter relaxation and a low residual.

frontHtml: Bladder pattern with cauda equina, sacral cord or diabetic neuropathy?
backHtml: Underactive detrusor with retention, large residual and overflow incontinence.

frontHtml: Mechanism of mirabegron and vibegron?
backHtml: Beta-3 agonists: G<sub>s</sub>, more cAMP, detrusor relaxation during storage; can raise blood pressure.

frontHtml: Urethral segment torn in pelvic fracture versus straddle injury?
backHtml: Pelvic fracture: posterior (membranous) urethra. Straddle injury: anterior (bulbar) urethra.

frontHtml: Why does urine from a bulbar urethral tear spread to the scrotum and abdominal wall but not the thighs?
backHtml: Colles (and Scarpa) fascia attach to the fascia lata.

frontHtml: Blow to a full bladder: where is the tear and what lab change can follow?
backHtml: The dome (intraperitoneal rupture); peritoneal reabsorption of urine raises serum urea nitrogen and creatinine.

frontHtml: Boy with oligohydramnios, thick bladder, dilated posterior urethra and bilateral hydronephrosis?
backHtml: Posterior urethral valves; confirm with voiding cystourethrography; endoscopic valve ablation.

frontHtml: Two causes of post-obstructive diuresis?
backHtml: Excretion of retained urea, salt and water, plus a temporary concentrating defect (medullary washout, less aquaporin-2).

frontHtml: Blood at the meatus after pelvic fracture: next step?
backHtml: Retrograde urethrogram before any urethral catheter; if disrupted, suprapubic cystostomy.

frontHtml: Extraperitoneal versus intraperitoneal bladder rupture: treatment?
backHtml: Extraperitoneal: catheter drainage about 2 weeks (most). Intraperitoneal: surgical repair.

frontHtml: Best test for suspected bladder rupture?
backHtml: CT (or conventional) cystography with retrograde filling to full distension.

frontHtml: Stable patient with high-grade renal laceration and no active bleeding: management?
backHtml: Nonoperative (admit, bed rest, serial hemoglobin); embolise active extravasation; operate for instability.

frontHtml: First-line treatment of stress urinary incontinence?
backHtml: Pelvic floor muscle training (and weight loss); then pessary or midurethral sling.

frontHtml: Preferred drug for overactive bladder in a frail or cognitively impaired older adult?
backHtml: A beta-3 agonist (mirabegron or vibegron) rather than an antimuscarinic.

frontHtml: Long-term management of an areflexic neurogenic bladder with a large residual?
backHtml: Clean intermittent catheterisation every 4–6 hours.

frontHtml: Secondary enuresis: what to check first?
backHtml: Urinalysis (glucose, specific gravity, infection) and history for constipation, sleep apnea and stress; diabetes mellitus and insipidus are causes.

frontHtml: Toddler after first febrile UTI: imaging order?
backHtml: Renal and bladder ultrasonography; voiding cystourethrography if abnormal or after a second febrile UTI.

frontHtml: Three embryonic kidneys and the fate of each?
backHtml: Pronephros regresses; mesonephros is interim and its duct becomes male ducts and gives the ureteric bud; metanephros is permanent (from week 5).

frontHtml: Ureteric bud derivatives?
backHtml: Ureter, renal pelvis, major and minor calyces, collecting ducts.

frontHtml: Which parts of the kidney come from the metanephric mesenchyme (metanephric blastema)?
backHtml: Everything from the glomerular capsule through the distal convoluted tubule, i.e. the nephron itself; the collecting system comes from the ureteric bud.

frontHtml: Signal that drives ureteric bud outgrowth?
backHtml: GDNF from the metanephric mesenchyme acting on RET on the bud.

frontHtml: What traps a horseshoe kidney, and which syndrome is associated?
backHtml: The inferior mesenteric artery; Turner syndrome (also trisomy 18).

frontHtml: Cause of death in Potter sequence?
backHtml: Pulmonary hypoplasia from oligohydramnios.

frontHtml: Commonest site of congenital urinary obstruction, and why?
backHtml: Ureteropelvic junction, the last part of the ureter to canalise (or a crossing vessel).

frontHtml: Complete duplex system: which ureter obstructs and which refluxes?
backHtml: Upper-pole ureter inserts low and medial and obstructs (ectopic, ureterocele); lower-pole ureter inserts high and lateral and refluxes.

frontHtml: Histology of multicystic dysplastic kidney?
backHtml: Noncommunicating cysts with primitive ducts in fibromuscular collars and islands of cartilage.

frontHtml: Urine from the umbilicus: which remnant, and what cancer later?
backHtml: Patent urachus (allantois); urachal adenocarcinoma at the bladder dome.

frontHtml: Bladder exstrophy: defect and associated findings?
backHtml: Failed infraumbilical mesoderm over the cloacal membrane; epispadias and pubic diastasis.

frontHtml: Mild unilateral prenatal hydronephrosis: when is the newborn scan?
backHtml: After about 48 hours of life; early only for bilateral disease or suspected valves.

frontHtml: Management of uncomplicated multicystic dysplastic kidney?
backHtml: Serial ultrasonography (involution, contralateral growth); check the other kidney; surgery only for complications.

frontHtml: Test of drainage and split function in suspected ureteropelvic junction obstruction?
backHtml: Diuretic renography (MAG3 with furosemide).

frontHtml: Indications for pyeloplasty?
backHtml: Symptoms, split function below about 40%, falling function or worsening dilation.

frontHtml: Girl always damp but voids normally: first test?
backHtml: Renal and bladder ultrasonography (duplex kidney with ectopic upper-pole ureter).

frontHtml: Renal screening in Turner syndrome?
backHtml: Renal ultrasonography at diagnosis for every patient.

frontHtml: ACE inhibitors and ARBs lower GFR by which arteriolar change?
backHtml: Dilating the efferent arteriole (removing angiotensin II tone), so glomerular pressure falls.

frontHtml: NSAIDs lower GFR by which arteriolar change, and in whom does it matter?
backHtml: Afferent constriction from lost prostaglandins; matters in heart failure, cirrhosis, volume depletion, CKD and older age.

frontHtml: Calcineurin inhibitors: renal hemodynamic effect and electrolyte effects?
backHtml: Afferent arteriolar constriction; hyperkalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypertension; chronic striped interstitial fibrosis.

frontHtml: How do aminoglycosides reach and injure proximal tubule cells?
backHtml: Bind megalin on the brush border, are endocytosed and accumulate in lysosomes; nonoliguric ATN after 5–10 days.

frontHtml: Cisplatin's signature electrolyte problem?
backHtml: Renal magnesium wasting (with ATN); prevent injury with vigorous saline hydration.

frontHtml: Tenofovir disoproxil kidney toxicity?
backHtml: Proximal tubulopathy: Fanconi syndrome (normoglycemic glycosuria, phosphaturia, proximal RTA); less with tenofovir alafenamide.

frontHtml: Amphotericin B: which RTA and which electrolytes fall?
backHtml: Distal (type 1) RTA with urine pH above 5.5; hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia.

frontHtml: How does lithium cause nephrogenic DI?
backHtml: Enters principal cells via ENaC and lowers aquaporin-2 expression.

frontHtml: Drugs that cause crystal nephropathy?
backHtml: IV acyclovir, methotrexate, sulfonamides (sulfadiazine), indinavir; prevent with hydration.

frontHtml: Classic drug causes of acute interstitial nephritis?
backHtml: Beta-lactams, PPIs, NSAIDs, sulfonamides, rifampin, allopurinol, immune checkpoint inhibitors.

frontHtml: Biopsy of drug-induced AIN?
backHtml: Interstitial edema with lymphocytes, plasma cells and eosinophils; tubulitis; normal glomeruli.

frontHtml: Heroin use is linked to which glomerular lesion?
backHtml: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.

frontHtml: Gadolinium in eGFR below 30 or dialysis can cause what?
backHtml: Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis: hardened skin of limbs and trunk with contractures; highest risk with linear agents.

frontHtml: Toxic metabolite and antidote for cyclophosphamide hemorrhagic cystitis?
backHtml: Acrolein; mesna (a thiol that binds it in urine) plus hydration.

frontHtml: Drug classes that cause urinary retention?
backHtml: Anticholinergics (antihistamines, tricyclics, antimuscarinics), alpha-1 agonists (decongestants) and opioids.

frontHtml: Proven ways to reduce contrast-associated AKI in a high-risk patient?
backHtml: Isotonic IV fluids before and after, lowest dose of low/iso-osmolar contrast, pause NSAIDs; N-acetylcysteine does not help.

frontHtml: Creatinine rise after starting an ACE inhibitor that is acceptable?
backHtml: Up to about 30%; continue the drug and recheck.

frontHtml: Creatinine up slightly on trimethoprim with unchanged BUN and bland urine?
backHtml: Blocked tubular creatinine secretion, not true AKI; cystatin C is unchanged.

frontHtml: Immune checkpoint inhibitor AIN: management?
backHtml: Hold the inhibitor and give prednisone (about 0.5–1 mg/kg/day) for moderate or worse injury.

frontHtml: Why does hypokalemia fail to correct on cisplatin?
backHtml: Hypomagnesemia keeps ROMK open and potassium is lost; replace magnesium.

frontHtml: Lithium nephrogenic DI when lithium must continue: drug?
backHtml: Amiloride (blocks ENaC lithium entry).

frontHtml: Acute urinary retention after starting diphenhydramine in a man with BPH: first step?
backHtml: Urethral catheter; then stop the drug and start an alpha-1 blocker.

frontHtml: Which product of proinsulin processing best reflects endogenous insulin secretion, and why?
backHtml: C-peptide: released in equal amounts with insulin, not cleared on first pass through the liver, longer half-life; absent from injected insulin.

frontHtml: Which beta-cell enzyme acts as the glucose sensor?
backHtml: Glucokinase (high Km, not inhibited by product). Loss of function causes GCK-MODY.

frontHtml: Sequence of glucose-stimulated insulin release?
backHtml: GLUT2 uptake → glucokinase → ↑ ATP/ADP → K-ATP channels close → depolarisation → Ca²⁺ influx → exocytosis.

frontHtml: Why does oral glucose release more insulin than the same IV glucose?
backHtml: Incretin effect: GLP-1 and GIP from the gut amplify glucose-dependent insulin secretion.

frontHtml: Islet histology: type 1 vs type 2 diabetes?
backHtml: Type 1: insulitis (lymphocytes) with beta-cell loss. Type 2: islet amyloid (amylin).

frontHtml: HLA types associated with type 1 diabetes?
backHtml: HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4 (DQ2 and DQ8).

frontHtml: Autoantibodies of type 1 diabetes?
backHtml: GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8 and insulin autoantibodies.

frontHtml: HNF1A-MODY: two clinical clues?
backHtml: Glycosuria from a low renal threshold and marked sensitivity to sulfonylureas.

frontHtml: Why do patients with HHS have little ketosis?
backHtml: Residual insulin restrains lipolysis and ketogenesis but not hepatic glucose output.

frontHtml: Serum potassium in DKA vs total-body potassium?
backHtml: Serum often normal or high (insulin lack, acidosis shift K⁺ out of cells); total-body K⁺ is depleted by urinary losses.

frontHtml: Enzyme that converts glucose to sorbitol, and tissues harmed?
backHtml: Aldose reductase; lens (cataract), Schwann cells (neuropathy), retina, kidney.

frontHtml: Kidney lesion specific for diabetic nephropathy?
backHtml: Nodular (Kimmelstiel-Wilson) glomerulosclerosis, with GBM thickening and hyaline arteriolosclerosis of afferent and efferent arterioles.

frontHtml: Sulfonylurea mechanism and main adverse effects?
backHtml: Bind SUR1 → close K-ATP → glucose-independent insulin release; hypoglycemia and weight gain.

frontHtml: Pioglitazone: mechanism and adverse effects?
backHtml: PPAR-gamma agonist (nuclear receptor with RXR); weight gain, fluid retention and heart failure, fractures.

frontHtml: SGLT2 inhibitor adverse effects?
backHtml: Genital mycotic infections, volume depletion, euglycemic DKA, rare perineal necrotising fasciitis.

frontHtml: GLP-1 receptor agonists are avoided with which history?
backHtml: Personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2 (also caution with prior pancreatitis).

frontHtml: Diagnostic thresholds for diabetes?
backHtml: A1c ≥ 6.5%; fasting glucose ≥ 126 mg/dL; 2-h OGTT ≥ 200 mg/dL; random ≥ 200 mg/dL with symptoms.

frontHtml: Two screening tests disagree (one diabetic, one not): next step?
backHtml: Repeat the test that was abnormal.

frontHtml: Type 2 diabetes with heart failure: preferred added drug class?
backHtml: SGLT2 inhibitor, regardless of A1c.

frontHtml: When is a less strict A1c target (about 8%) appropriate?
backHtml: Older adults with multiple illnesses, cognitive impairment, falls or limited life expectancy.

frontHtml: When to start retinopathy screening in type 1 vs type 2 diabetes?
backHtml: Type 1: within 5 years of onset. Type 2: at diagnosis. Then every 1–2 years if normal.

frontHtml: Key treatment for a noninfected neuropathic diabetic foot ulcer?
backHtml: Offloading (total contact cast or walker) plus debridement.

frontHtml: DKA or HHS with K⁺ below 3.3 mEq/L: what first?
backHtml: Hold insulin; give IV potassium until at least 3.3 mEq/L.

frontHtml: When is dextrose added to fluids in DKA and HHS?
backHtml: DKA: glucose about 250 mg/dL. HHS: about 300 mg/dL. Keep insulin running.

frontHtml: How to stop an insulin infusion after DKA resolves?
backHtml: Give subcutaneous basal insulin 1–2 hours before stopping the infusion.

frontHtml: Sick-day rule for basal insulin in type 1 diabetes?
backHtml: Never stop it; monitor glucose and ketones and use correction doses.

frontHtml: Drugs to stop before pregnancy in a woman with diabetes?
backHtml: ACE inhibitors/ARBs and statins; start folic acid and aim for A1c below 6.5% if safe.

frontHtml: Whipple's triad?
backHtml: Symptoms of hypoglycemia, a low plasma glucose measured at the time (below 55 mg/dL in people without diabetes), and relief when glucose is raised.

frontHtml: Order of the counterregulatory response to falling glucose?
backHtml: Insulin secretion stops, then glucagon rises, then epinephrine; cortisol and growth hormone act over hours.

frontHtml: Why does C-peptide separate injected insulin from the body's own insulin?
backHtml: C-peptide is cleaved from proinsulin inside beta cells and released with insulin; drug insulin contains none.

frontHtml: High insulin, high C-peptide, high proinsulin: two possible causes?
backHtml: Insulinoma or an insulin secretagogue (sulfonylurea, meglitinide); a drug screen separates them.

frontHtml: Low insulin, low C-peptide and low ketones during hypoglycemia with a large tumour?
backHtml: Non-islet cell tumour hypoglycemia from incompletely processed ("big") IGF-2.

frontHtml: How does alcohol cause fasting hypoglycemia?
backHtml: A high NADH/NAD<sup>+</sup> ratio diverts pyruvate and oxaloacetate away from gluconeogenesis once glycogen is depleted.

frontHtml: Necrolytic migratory erythema, new diabetes, weight loss and DVT?
backHtml: Glucagonoma (alpha-cell tumour).

frontHtml: Watery diarrhea despite fasting, hypokalemia, achlorhydria?
backHtml: VIPoma: VIP raises enterocyte cAMP and drives chloride secretion.

frontHtml: Somatostatinoma triad?
backHtml: Diabetes, gallstones and steatorrhea (with achlorhydria).

frontHtml: Why do infants of mothers with diabetes become hypoglycemic after birth?
backHtml: Fetal beta-cell hyperplasia keeps secreting insulin after the maternal glucose supply stops.

frontHtml: Hypoglycemia in a conscious patient who can swallow?
backHtml: 15–20 g fast-acting carbohydrate; recheck after 15 minutes; repeat if low; then eat.

frontHtml: Hypoglycemia in a person who cannot swallow, outside hospital?
backHtml: Glucagon (IM, SC or intranasal) and recovery position; nothing by mouth.

frontHtml: Recurrent hypoglycemia from a sulfonylurea despite dextrose: added drug?
backHtml: Octreotide (inhibits insulin secretion); admit for monitoring.

frontHtml: Management of hypoglycemia unawareness in type 1 diabetes?
backHtml: CGM with alerts, insulin review, and weeks of strict hypoglycemia avoidance with higher targets.

frontHtml: Post-bariatric hypoglycemia: timing and first-line treatment?
backHtml: 1–3 hours after meals; small frequent meals low in refined carbohydrate (then acarbose).

frontHtml: When is the pancreas imaged in suspected insulinoma?
backHtml: Only after endogenous hyperinsulinism is proven and the secretagogue screen is negative: CT or MRI, then EUS.

frontHtml: Drug that controls insulinoma hypoglycemia when surgery is not possible?
backHtml: Diazoxide (opens beta-cell K<sub>ATP</sub> channels), or a somatostatin analogue.

frontHtml: Embryologic origin of the thyroid and the clue to a thyroglossal duct cyst?
backHtml: Foramen cecum of the tongue; a midline neck mass that rises with tongue protrusion or swallowing.

frontHtml: Which enzyme performs both organification and coupling?
backHtml: Thyroid peroxidase (TPO), the target of methimazole and PTU.

frontHtml: What does the sodium-iodide symporter do, and what blocks it?
backHtml: Concentrates iodide into follicular cells; perchlorate and pertechnetate compete with it.

frontHtml: Wolff-Chaikoff effect?
backHtml: A large iodide load transiently inhibits organification; normal glands escape within days.

frontHtml: Estrogen or pregnancy: effect on total T4, free T4 and TSH?
backHtml: TBG rises: total T4 high, free T4 and TSH normal.

frontHtml: Extra action of PTU compared with methimazole?
backHtml: Inhibits peripheral 5′-deiodinase (T4 to T3).

frontHtml: Two serious PTU-specific adverse effects?
backHtml: Severe hepatocellular injury and ANCA-associated vasculitis (plus agranulocytosis, shared with methimazole).

frontHtml: Methimazole embryopathy?
backHtml: First-trimester exposure: aplasia cutis, choanal or esophageal atresia; so use PTU in the first trimester.

frontHtml: How does lithium cause hypothyroidism?
backHtml: It inhibits thyroid hormone release (and causes goiter).

frontHtml: Hashimoto histology?
backHtml: Lymphoid follicles with germinal centres, atrophic follicles and Hürthle (oncocytic) cells.

frontHtml: Which malignancy is more likely after years of Hashimoto thyroiditis?
backHtml: Primary lymphoma of the thyroid, a B-cell tumour (diffuse large B-cell or marginal-zone/MALT type); suspect it when the gland enlarges quickly.

frontHtml: Mechanism of Graves orbitopathy?
backHtml: TSH-receptor-bearing orbital fibroblasts make glycosaminoglycans and fat, swelling muscles (tendons spared) and orbital fat.

frontHtml: Painful thyroid after a viral illness, high ESR, low uptake?
backHtml: Subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis: granulomas with giant cells; NSAIDs and β-blocker.

frontHtml: Rock-hard, fixed thyroid with fibrosis into neck tissues?
backHtml: Riedel thyroiditis, part of IgG4-related disease.

frontHtml: Papillary carcinoma features?
backHtml: Clear grooved nuclei with pseudoinclusions, psammoma bodies; BRAF V600E or RET/PTC; lymphatic spread; good prognosis.

frontHtml: What defines follicular carcinoma versus adenoma?
backHtml: Capsular or vascular invasion (so FNA cannot tell them apart); spreads hematogenously.

frontHtml: Medullary carcinoma: cell, stroma, markers?
backHtml: Parafollicular C cells; amyloid from calcitonin; calcitonin and CEA; RET.

frontHtml: Thyroid hormone pattern in euthyroid sick syndrome?
backHtml: Low T3, high reverse T3, normal or low TSH and T4; don't treat.

frontHtml: Best single screening test for primary thyroid disease, and when it fails?
backHtml: TSH; it fails in pituitary or hypothalamic disease, where free T4 is followed.

frontHtml: Thyrotoxicosis with low radioiodine uptake: causes and the test that splits them?
backHtml: Thyroiditis, exogenous hormone, iodine load; thyroglobulin is high in thyroiditis and low with exogenous hormone.

frontHtml: Levothyroxine on confirmed pregnancy?
backHtml: Increase the dose by about 25–30% straight away; check TSH about every 4 weeks in the first half.

frontHtml: When is subclinical hypothyroidism treated?
backHtml: Persistent TSH of 10 or more; individualise below that (symptoms, anti-TPO, pregnancy plans). Repeat testing first.

frontHtml: Myxedema coma treatment?
backHtml: IV levothyroxine with IV hydrocortisone, ventilatory support, passive rewarming, ICU.

frontHtml: Thyroid storm drug order?
backHtml: β-blocker, then PTU, then iodine at least 1 hour later, plus hydrocortisone; avoid aspirin.

frontHtml: Fever and sore throat on methimazole?
backHtml: Stop it and check a CBC with differential; do not switch to PTU.

frontHtml: When is radioiodine avoided in Graves disease?
backHtml: Pregnancy, breastfeeding and moderate-to-severe active orbitopathy.

frontHtml: First test for a thyroid nodule, and what if it is low?
backHtml: TSH; if low, radionuclide scan (a hot nodule needs no FNA).

frontHtml: Benign (Bethesda II) FNA in a low- or intermediate-suspicion nodule?
backHtml: Ultrasound surveillance at about 12–24 months; repeat FNA only for growth or new suspicious features.

frontHtml: Tumour marker after total thyroidectomy for differentiated cancer?
backHtml: Thyroglobulin.

frontHtml: Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis types and treatment?
backHtml: Type 1 (iodine-driven synthesis): thionamide; type 2 (destructive): glucocorticoids.

frontHtml: Supplement that falsely mimics Graves on immunoassays?
backHtml: Biotin; stop it for a few days and retest.

frontHtml: First test after confirming true hypercalcemia?
backHtml: Intact PTH: high or inappropriately normal is PTH-dependent (primary hyperparathyroidism, FHH, lithium); suppressed means look for PTHrP, calcitriol, myeloma or metastases.

frontHtml: PTH actions on the kidney?
backHtml: More calcium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule, less phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule, more 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity.

frontHtml: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia: gene, inheritance and urine finding?
backHtml: Heterozygous loss-of-function CASR, autosomal dominant; calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio below 0.01. Benign; no surgery.

frontHtml: Which hormone lowers phosphate and suppresses 1-alpha-hydroxylase, rising early in CKD?
backHtml: FGF23 (from osteocytes).

frontHtml: Why does severe hypomagnesemia cause hypocalcemia?
backHtml: Magnesium is needed for PTH secretion and for PTH action on bone and kidney; replace magnesium first.

frontHtml: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A: defect and labs?
backHtml: Maternally inherited GNAS (Gs-alpha) loss; low calcium, high phosphate, high PTH, with Albright hereditary osteodystrophy.

frontHtml: Same GNAS variant inherited from the father?
backHtml: Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism: Albright features with normal calcium and PTH.

frontHtml: Osteomalacia labs?
backHtml: Calcium low or normal, phosphate low, alkaline phosphatase high, PTH high, 25-hydroxyvitamin D usually low; histology shows wide osteoid seams.

frontHtml: Paget disease: lab hallmark and histology?
backHtml: Isolated high alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium and phosphate; mosaic lamellar bone with cement lines.

frontHtml: Mechanism of denosumab?
backHtml: Monoclonal antibody against RANKL, blocking osteoclast formation and activation.

frontHtml: Why is intermittent teriparatide anabolic when continuous PTH excess resorbs bone?
backHtml: Daily pulses favour osteoblast activity over osteoclast activation; sustained PTH drives RANKL-mediated resorption.

frontHtml: Acute treatment of severe hypercalcemia?
backHtml: IV isotonic saline, calcitonin (rapid, short-lived), IV zoledronic acid (sustained); denosumab if kidney function bars bisphosphonates.

frontHtml: Surgical criteria in asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism?
backHtml: Calcium >1 mg/dL above normal; T-score ≤ −2.5 or vertebral fracture; eGFR <60, stones, nephrocalcinosis or hypercalciuria; age <50.

frontHtml: Role of a sestamibi scan in primary hyperparathyroidism?
backHtml: Localisation before surgery only; the diagnosis is biochemical.

frontHtml: Hypercalcemia with high 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and suppressed PTH: treatment?
backHtml: Glucocorticoids (granulomatous disease or lymphoma), plus treat the cause.

frontHtml: Which vitamin D form for chronic hypoparathyroidism, and what calcium target?
backHtml: Calcitriol; aim for low-normal serum calcium to limit hypercalciuria.

frontHtml: Who should be screened for osteoporosis?
backHtml: All women 65 and older; younger postmenopausal women at increased risk.

frontHtml: What must follow when denosumab is stopped?
backHtml: A bisphosphonate, to prevent rebound bone loss and multiple vertebral fractures.

frontHtml: Adrenal cortex zones and products, outside in?
backHtml: Glomerulosa: aldosterone (angiotensin II, potassium). Fasciculata: cortisol (ACTH). Reticularis: androgen precursors (ACTH).

frontHtml: Why does primary adrenal insufficiency cause hyperpigmentation?
backHtml: Low cortisol removes feedback, so POMC rises; its products ACTH and MSH stimulate melanocortin-1 receptors.

frontHtml: Which electrolyte finding separates primary from secondary adrenal insufficiency?
backHtml: Hyperkalemia: only primary disease loses aldosterone; in secondary disease renin-angiotensin still drives aldosterone.

frontHtml: Most common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency in high-income countries, and worldwide?
backHtml: Autoimmune adrenalitis (21-hydroxylase antibodies); tuberculosis worldwide.

frontHtml: Cushing syndrome with suppressed ACTH: where is the problem?
backHtml: Adrenal (adenoma or carcinoma) or exogenous glucocorticoid.

frontHtml: Very high ACTH, no suppression with high-dose dexamethasone, hypokalemia, in a smoker?
backHtml: Ectopic ACTH, most often small cell lung carcinoma.

frontHtml: Hypertension and hypokalemia with low renin and low aldosterone: three causes?
backHtml: Liddle syndrome, apparent mineralocorticoid excess (or licorice), 11β- or 17α-hydroxylase deficiency.

frontHtml: How does licorice cause hypertension?
backHtml: Glycyrrhetinic acid inhibits 11β-HSD2, so cortisol activates the renal mineralocorticoid receptor.

frontHtml: Neuroblastoma: marker of poor prognosis and urine tests?
backHtml: MYCN amplification; raised urine HVA and VMA.

frontHtml: Germline variant frequency in pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma?
backHtml: Roughly a third or more (RET, VHL, NF1, SDH genes), so offer genetic testing to all.

frontHtml: First step in suspected adrenal crisis?
backHtml: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV plus isotonic saline (and dextrose), without waiting for tests.

frontHtml: Confirmatory test for adrenal insufficiency in a stable patient?
backHtml: Cosyntropin stimulation: peak cortisol below about 18 µg/dL (about 14–15 with newer assays) is abnormal.

frontHtml: Treatment of primary adrenal insufficiency?
backHtml: Hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone, sick-day rules, injectable emergency hydrocortisone, medical ID.

frontHtml: Screening tests for Cushing syndrome?
backHtml: Late-night salivary cortisol, 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression, 24-hour urine free cortisol (two abnormal to confirm).

frontHtml: ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome with no adenoma on pituitary MRI: next test?
backHtml: Inferior petrosal sinus sampling with CRH or desmopressin stimulation.

frontHtml: Primary aldosteronism: screening test?
backHtml: Plasma aldosterone with renin: high aldosterone with suppressed renin; correct hypokalemia first.

frontHtml: Before adrenalectomy for primary aldosteronism, how is the side confirmed?
backHtml: Adrenal vein sampling (CT nodules are often nonfunctioning).

frontHtml: Medical treatment of bilateral adrenal hyperplasia causing aldosteronism?
backHtml: Spironolactone or eplerenone, titrated until renin rises.

frontHtml: Best biochemical test for pheochromocytoma?
backHtml: Plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urine fractionated metanephrines.

frontHtml: Preoperative preparation for pheochromocytoma?
backHtml: Alpha blockade (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) for 1–2 weeks with salt and fluids; beta blocker only afterwards.

frontHtml: Hormone tests for every adrenal incidentaloma?
backHtml: 1-mg dexamethasone suppression test; metanephrines unless clearly a lipid-rich adenoma; aldosterone and renin if hypertension or hypokalemia.

frontHtml: Adrenal mass under 4 cm, homogeneous, 10 HU or less, nonfunctioning: follow-up?
backHtml: None needed: lipid-rich adenoma.

frontHtml: Central precocious puberty in a boy: required test?
backHtml: Brain MRI (hypothalamic hamartoma and other CNS lesions).

frontHtml: Triad of McCune-Albright syndrome?
backHtml: Peripheral precocious puberty, irregular café-au-lait macules, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia (mosaic activating GNAS).

frontHtml: Most common cause of delayed puberty?
backHtml: Constitutional delay: short, delayed bone age, family history of late maturation.

frontHtml: Embryologic origin of the anterior vs posterior pituitary?
backHtml: Anterior: Rathke pouch (oral surface ectoderm). Posterior: diencephalon floor (neuroectoderm).

frontHtml: Why does a nonfunctioning macroadenoma raise prolactin modestly?
backHtml: Stalk effect: dopamine from the arcuate nucleus can no longer reach lactotrophs.

frontHtml: Order in which pituitary axes usually fail with a growing mass?
backHtml: GH, then LH/FSH, then TSH, then ACTH.

frontHtml: Visual field defect from a pituitary macroadenoma pressing on the chiasm?
backHtml: Bitemporal hemianopia (crossing nasal retinal fibres).

frontHtml: Calcified, cystic suprasellar mass with oily fluid in a child?
backHtml: Craniopharyngioma, from Rathke pouch remnants (adamantinomatous type: beta-catenin mutations).

frontHtml: Earliest sign of Sheehan syndrome?
backHtml: Failure to lactate after severe postpartum hemorrhage.

frontHtml: Pegvisomant: mechanism and monitoring test?
backHtml: GH receptor antagonist; monitor IGF-1 (GH levels rise).

frontHtml: Very large prolactinoma with only a modestly raised prolactin result: what assay pitfall?
backHtml: Hook effect; repeat on a diluted sample.

frontHtml: First-line treatment of a macroprolactinoma with visual field loss?
backHtml: Cabergoline (dopamine agonist); surgery if resistant, intolerant or apoplexy.

frontHtml: Acromegaly: screening test and confirmatory test?
backHtml: Screen: IGF-1. Confirm: GH fails to suppress after an oral glucose load. Then MRI.

frontHtml: Pituitary apoplexy: first treatment?
backHtml: Stress-dose IV hydrocortisone, then urgent neurosurgical review.

frontHtml: Hypopituitarism: which hormone is replaced first?
backHtml: Cortisol, before levothyroxine (thyroid hormone can precipitate adrenal crisis).

frontHtml: How do you dose levothyroxine in central hypothyroidism?
backHtml: By free T4; TSH is unreliable.

frontHtml: Water deprivation test: central DI pattern?
backHtml: Urine stays dilute with dehydration, then rises sharply (often more than 50%) after desmopressin.

frontHtml: SIADH diagnostic criteria (labs)?
backHtml: Hypotonic hyponatremia, euvolemia, urine osmolality above about 100 mOsm/kg, urine sodium above about 30 mEq/L, normal thyroid and adrenal function, no diuretics.

frontHtml: Maximum sodium rise in chronic hyponatremia in a high-risk patient?
backHtml: About 8 mEq/L in 24 hours, to avoid osmotic demyelination.

frontHtml: Constitutional delay of growth vs familial short stature: bone age?
backHtml: Constitutional delay: bone age delayed. Familial short stature: bone age equals chronological age.

frontHtml: Which hypothalamic nucleus mainly makes ADH, and which mainly makes oxytocin?
backHtml: ADH: supraoptic. Oxytocin: paraventricular. Both are released from the posterior pituitary.

frontHtml: Lesion of the ventromedial vs lateral hypothalamus?
backHtml: Ventromedial: hyperphagia and obesity. Lateral: anorexia and weight loss.

frontHtml: Lesion of the anterior vs posterior hypothalamus (temperature)?
backHtml: Anterior: hyperthermia (no heat loss). Posterior: poikilothermia.

frontHtml: Suprachiasmatic nucleus function?
backHtml: Circadian clock, driven by light via the retinohypothalamic tract; controls melatonin rhythm.

frontHtml: Satiety pathway from leptin?
backHtml: Leptin → arcuate POMC neurons → alpha-MSH → MC4R (paraventricular) → satiety.

frontHtml: Commonest single-gene cause of severe early-onset obesity?
backHtml: Loss-of-function MC4R variants.

frontHtml: Kallmann syndrome: cause and key findings?
backHtml: Failed GnRH neuron migration from the olfactory placode: anosmia, low LH/FSH and sex steroids.

frontHtml: Pulsatile vs continuous GnRH?
backHtml: Pulsatile stimulates LH/FSH; continuous (depot agonist) suppresses them.

frontHtml: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea hormone pattern?
backHtml: Low or normal LH and FSH, low estradiol, normal prolactin and TSH.

frontHtml: Gelastic seizures plus central precocious puberty?
backHtml: Hypothalamic hamartoma (contains GnRH neurons).

frontHtml: Child with lytic skull lesions, scalp rash and central DI?
backHtml: Langerhans cell histiocytosis (CD1a, langerin, Birbeck granules).

frontHtml: First-line treatment of functional hypothalamic amenorrhea?
backHtml: Restore energy balance: more calories, less training, nutrition and psychological support.

frontHtml: Bone protection if menses do not return in functional hypothalamic amenorrhea?
backHtml: Short-term transdermal estradiol with cyclic oral progestin; not the combined pill or bisphosphonates.

frontHtml: Man with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism wants fertility: treatment?
backHtml: Stop testosterone; give hCG, adding FSH if needed (or pulsatile GnRH).

frontHtml: Common drug cause of secondary hypogonadism in men?
backHtml: Long-term opioids (GnRH suppression); also glucocorticoids and anabolic steroids.

frontHtml: Central precocious puberty: who needs brain MRI?
backHtml: All boys, and girls who are very young (especially under 6) or have neurologic signs.

frontHtml: Triphasic response after pituitary or hypothalamic surgery?
backHtml: Diabetes insipidus, then SIADH-like phase (about a week later), then permanent DI.

frontHtml: MEN1: gene, protein and mechanism?
backHtml: MEN1 on 11q13, menin; tumour suppressor, loss of function (two hits).

frontHtml: Three main tumour sites in MEN1?
backHtml: Parathyroid hyperplasia, pancreatic/duodenal neuroendocrine tumours, anterior pituitary adenomas (mostly prolactinoma).

frontHtml: Usually the first manifestation of MEN1?
backHtml: Primary hyperparathyroidism from multigland hyperplasia.

frontHtml: MEN2: gene and mechanism?
backHtml: RET proto-oncogene (receptor tyrosine kinase) on 10q11; gain of function, one hit.

frontHtml: MEN2A components?
backHtml: Medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, parathyroid hyperplasia; also cutaneous lichen amyloidosis and Hirschsprung disease in some families.

frontHtml: MEN2B components?
backHtml: MTC (earliest, most aggressive), pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas, intestinal ganglioneuromatosis, marfanoid habitus; no hyperparathyroidism.

frontHtml: Cell of origin and markers of medullary thyroid carcinoma?
backHtml: Neural crest-derived parafollicular C cells; calcitonin and CEA; amyloid stroma from calcitonin.

frontHtml: Why is radioiodine useless in medullary thyroid carcinoma?
backHtml: C cells do not concentrate iodine (and are not TSH-dependent).

frontHtml: Who gets germline RET testing?
backHtml: Every patient with MTC, anyone with MEN2 features, and relatives of known carriers.

frontHtml: First test before surgery in a patient with MTC or a RET variant?
backHtml: Plasma free (or urine fractionated) metanephrines to exclude pheochromocytoma.

frontHtml: Order of surgery in MEN2 with pheochromocytoma and MTC?
backHtml: Alpha-blockade, adrenalectomy, then total thyroidectomy.

frontHtml: Timing of prophylactic thyroidectomy by RET risk?
backHtml: M918T (MEN2B): first year of life; codon 634: at or before about age 5, by calcitonin; moderate risk: when calcitonin rises.

frontHtml: Parathyroid operation for MEN1 hyperparathyroidism?
backHtml: Subtotal (three-and-a-half gland) or total parathyroidectomy with autotransplant, plus transcervical thymectomy.

frontHtml: Levothyroxine goal after thyroidectomy for MTC?
backHtml: Normal TSH (replacement); no TSH suppression.

frontHtml: Why does treating hyperparathyroidism help Zollinger-Ellison syndrome in MEN1?
backHtml: Hypercalcemia stimulates gastrin release; normal calcium lowers gastrin and acid output.

frontHtml: Which gene starts testis development?
backHtml: SRY on the Y chromosome.

frontHtml: What does anti-Müllerian hormone do, and which cell makes it?
backHtml: Sertoli cells; it causes regression of the Müllerian ducts (no uterus, tubes or upper vagina).

frontHtml: Which hormone forms male external genitalia and prostate?
backHtml: Dihydrotestosterone, made from testosterone by 5α-reductase type 2.

frontHtml: 46,XY, female at birth, virilises at puberty, normal testosterone, high testosterone-to-DHT ratio?
backHtml: 5α-reductase type 2 deficiency.

frontHtml: Complete androgen insensitivity: internal and external anatomy?
backHtml: Testes, no uterus, no Wolffian structures; female external genitalia, breasts at puberty, sparse pubic and axillary hair.

frontHtml: Most common CAH enzyme and its electrolyte picture?
backHtml: 21-hydroxylase (about 95%); salt wasting with hyponatremia and hyperkalemia in the classic form.

frontHtml: CAH forms that cause hypertension?
backHtml: 11β-hydroxylase (with virilisation) and 17α-hydroxylase (with absent sex steroids), from excess 11-deoxycorticosterone.

frontHtml: Commonest cause of congenital hypothyroidism where iodine intake is adequate?
backHtml: Thyroid dysgenesis (aplasia, hypoplasia or ectopic gland).

frontHtml: Why do most hypothyroid newborns look normal at birth?
backHtml: Maternal T4 crosses the placenta.

frontHtml: Signs of untreated congenital hypothyroidism?
backHtml: Prolonged jaundice, poor feeding, constipation, hypotonia, large tongue, umbilical hernia, large posterior fontanelle.

frontHtml: Kallmann syndrome mechanism and clues?
backHtml: Failed migration of GnRH neurons from the olfactory placode: hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia.

frontHtml: Virilised newborn with nonpalpable gonads: most likely diagnosis and urgent tests?
backHtml: 46,XX with 21-hydroxylase CAH; electrolytes, glucose, 17-hydroxyprogesterone, karyotype, pelvic ultrasonography.

frontHtml: When is sex assigned in a newborn with atypical genitalia?
backHtml: After the evaluation, with a multidisciplinary team; not on appearance alone.

frontHtml: Why is newborn 17-hydroxyprogesterone hard to interpret in preterm infants?
backHtml: It is physiologically higher in preterm, sick or stressed infants and early samples; cut-offs are adjusted for birth weight or gestational age.

frontHtml: Treatment of salt-wasting CAH crisis?
backHtml: IV isotonic saline, dextrose and stress-dose hydrocortisone.

frontHtml: Glucocorticoid of choice for children with CAH, and why?
backHtml: Hydrocortisone: least growth-suppressive.

frontHtml: Levothyroxine starting dose in congenital hypothyroidism?
backHtml: 10–15 µg/kg/day, started as soon as confirmatory blood is drawn, ideally within 2 weeks of birth.

frontHtml: How should infant levothyroxine be given?
backHtml: Crushed in a small volume by spoon; separate from soy formula, iron and calcium.

frontHtml: First evaluation after diagnosing Turner syndrome?
backHtml: Cardiac and aortic imaging (bicuspid valve, coarctation, aortic dilation), plus renal ultrasonography.

frontHtml: Hypospadias with an undescended testis: what to do before surgery?
backHtml: DSD evaluation; postpone circumcision.

frontHtml: After how long on a supraphysiologic glucocorticoid dose should HPA suppression be assumed?
backHtml: About 3 weeks or more (also evening dosing or cushingoid features); taper rather than stop.

frontHtml: Why is potassium usually normal in adrenal insufficiency after stopping glucocorticoids?
backHtml: It is secondary (ACTH-deficient); aldosterone is controlled by renin-angiotensin and is preserved.

frontHtml: Anabolic steroid use: LH, FSH and testis size?
backHtml: LH and FSH suppressed; small testes, azoospermia; also erythrocytosis and low HDL.

frontHtml: Amiodarone hypothyroidism mechanism?
backHtml: Iodine excess inhibits organification (Wolff-Chaikoff effect) and an autoimmune-damaged gland fails to escape.

frontHtml: Type 1 versus type 2 amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis?
backHtml: Type 1: iodine-fuelled synthesis in nodular or Graves gland (methimazole). Type 2: destructive thyroiditis in a normal gland (glucocorticoids).

frontHtml: How does lithium cause hypercalcemia?
backHtml: Raises the CaSR set point, so PTH is high or inappropriately normal; it can also lead to parathyroid hyperplasia or adenoma.

frontHtml: Which checkpoint inhibitor class most often causes hypophysitis, and which thyroiditis?
backHtml: Anti-CTLA-4 (ipilimumab): hypophysitis. Anti-PD-1/PD-L1 (nivolumab, pembrolizumab): thyroiditis.

frontHtml: Enzyme inhibited by etomidate and metyrapone?
backHtml: 11-beta-hydroxylase: cortisol falls, 11-deoxycortisol rises.

frontHtml: Why do SGLT2 inhibitors cause euglycemic DKA?
backHtml: Glucosuria keeps glucose low, insulin falls and glucagon rises, so ketogenesis proceeds with near-normal glucose.

frontHtml: Thiazide hyperglycemia mechanism?
backHtml: Hypokalemia reduces insulin secretion from beta cells.

frontHtml: Antipsychotic galactorrhea: pathway?
backHtml: D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway removes dopamine inhibition of prolactin.

frontHtml: Suspected adrenal crisis: first treatment?
backHtml: IV hydrocortisone at once with isotonic saline and dextrose; draw cortisol first only if it causes no delay.

frontHtml: Sick-day rules for patients on long-term glucocorticoids?
backHtml: Double or triple the dose during febrile illness, injectable hydrocortisone if vomiting, medical identification, stress dosing for surgery.

frontHtml: Checkpoint-inhibitor thyroiditis management?
backHtml: Beta-blocker for the thyrotoxic phase, continue immunotherapy, monitor for hypothyroidism and start levothyroxine when it appears.

frontHtml: Hypophysitis with low cortisol and low free T4: which hormone first?
backHtml: Glucocorticoid before levothyroxine, to avoid precipitating adrenal crisis.

frontHtml: Checkpoint-inhibitor diabetes treatment?
backHtml: Insulin; it is permanent and not reversed by glucocorticoids.

frontHtml: Biotin effect on thyroid immunoassays?
backHtml: Falsely low TSH (sandwich assay) and falsely high free T4 and T3 (competitive assays); stop biotin 2–3 days and repeat.

frontHtml: Why is radioiodine ineffective soon after iodinated contrast?
backHtml: The iodine load saturates the gland, so tracer uptake is suppressed for weeks.
